answer.label: Not Epicurus’s exact words — a modern paraphrase of Principal Doctrine 27
answer.authorDates: 341–270 BCE · Greek philosopher, founder of Epicureanism
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Epicurus’s — it compresses Principal Doctrine 27, preserved in Diogenes Laertius’s Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book X ↗. But this exact one-liner appears in no standard translation: the R. D. Hicks rendering ↗ reads “Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to ensure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.” The short form is a web-era condensation, not Epicurus’s translated words.

source.excerpt: Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to ensure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.
trail: The idea comes from Epicurus’s Principal Doctrines ↗, a list of core maxims preserved by Diogenes Laertius in Book X of his Lives.
The standard English of maxim 27 — Hicks 1925 ↗ and Bailey 1926 ↗ — is a full sentence, not this compressed slogan.
Wikiquote ↗ carries the full maxim; the short one-liner does not appear verbatim in any sourced edition.
source.excerptNote: Principal Doctrine 27 in R. D. Hicks’s 1925 translation, as presented by the Internet Classics Archive. The popular short form drops “which are procured by wisdom” and “throughout the whole of life,” and swaps “the acquisition of friends” for “friendship.”

author.bio: Epicurus (341–270 BCE) was a Greek philosopher who founded his school, the Garden, in Athens around 307/06 BCE. He taught that a tranquil, pleasant life is the highest good, and he placed an exceptionally high value on friendship (philia) as essential to human happiness and security. His writings survive mainly in fragments and in the summaries and maxim-lists preserved by the later biographer Diogenes Laertius.

misattribution.heading: A real idea, a paraphrased wording
misattribution.intro: This is not a false attribution of the idea — friendship’s primacy really is Epicurean doctrine. It is a misquote: the popular sentence is a modern rewrite that no published translator wrote.

items.why: “Of all the means to ensure happiness, friendship is the most important” compresses Principal Doctrine 27 ↗, cutting “which are procured by wisdom” and “throughout the whole of life” and replacing “the acquisition of friends” with “friendship.” No standard translation reads this way.

items.who: Editions that cite it as PD 28
items.why: Most editions, including the Internet Classics Archive ↗, number this doctrine 27; a few sources (e.g. some Wikiquote ↗ listings) number it 28.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine text, per Hicks’s translation ↗ of Principal Doctrine 27, is “Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to ensure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.”

context.heading: Why friendship sat at the center of Epicurus’s ethics
lead: For Epicurus, the goal of life was ataraxia — freedom from anxiety — and he argued that secure, trusting friendships were among the surest supports of a tranquil life. As the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy ↗ notes, he “placed an extremely high value on friendship,” even holding that a wise person would suffer for a friend as for themselves.

That is why the sentiment resonates so widely today — it is authentically Epicurean. The friction is only in the words: the crisp modern slogan is easier to share than the fuller ancient maxim, so the paraphrase has largely displaced the translation.
detailsBody: The Principal Doctrines (Kyriai Doxai) are forty short maxims summarizing Epicurean ethics. They survive because Diogenes Laertius quoted the whole set in Book X of his Lives of Eminent Philosophers, written centuries after Epicurus’s death.
context.pull: The idea is real Epicurus; the exact sentence is not.
